title: Meituan-Robotics-0: A Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Desktop Manipulation
summary: We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. MR0 combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. A three-stage training recipe aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior through discrete action-token pre-training, transfers these priors to continuous cross-embodiment control through flow-matching mid-training, and adapts the policy through real-world post-training. We introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections to provide positive and negative supervision for CFG-DAgger without value learning or advantage labeling. A unified end-effector interface supports heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. An event-driven agent maintains persistent task events and reassesses plans when progress or feasibility changes, enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than $π_{0.5}$ across three real-robot tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90. Qualitative agent deployments demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions.
full_text: General-purpose desktop manipulation requires an embodied system that can acquire broad behavioral priors from heterogeneous data, transfer them across robot embodiments, recover from closed-loop execution errors, and preserve task-relevant state over extended horizons. We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. Its data foundation combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. MR0 converts this heterogeneous experience into executable control through a three-stage training recipe. Discrete action-token pre-training first aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior. Continuous flow-matching mid-training then transfers these priors to fine-grained cross-embodiment control. Real-world post-training further adapts the policy using successful demonstrations, human-gated corrections, and outcome-labeled autonomous rollouts. We introduce Rollback, a data collection mechanism that pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections for CFG-DAgger training. A unified end-effector interface supports learning across heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. Because the low-level policy is reactive, an event-driven agent converts visual observations into persistent task events and invokes task-level reassessment only when task progress or feasibility changes. This separation preserves continuous motor control while enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. Evaluated as a standalone policy, MR0 achieves 93.6 success on RoboTwin~2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than across the three tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70 success and a progress score of 0.90 without value learning or advantage labeling. Qualitative agent deployments further demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions. These results show that aligned heterogeneous data, real-world post-training, and event-level memory provide complementary foundations for transferable and long-horizon desktop manipulation. Their increasing data and model scales have substantially broadened the range of manipulation behaviors that can be learned within a single policy. Deploying such policies on desktop manipulation, however, exposes several limitations that cannot be addressed by scaling the action model alone. Robot datasets~ agibotworld,galaxea,khazatsky2024droid,tian2025interndata,robocoin2025,zhang2026hy,wang2026robointer1 collected from different sources use inconsistent observation formats, action spaces, embodiments, and task descriptions, which prevents them from providing coherent supervision without careful alignment. Even after data alignment, policies trained primarily on successful demonstrations receive little guidance for recovering from the error states induced by their own closed-loop behavior. Moreover, a reactive policy conditioned only on the current observation cannot preserve task information once it leaves the observation window. A practical desktop-manipulation system must therefore connect aligned heterogeneous data, robust real-world policy learning, and persistent task-level memory. We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a desktop-manipulation framework built around a large-scale data foundation, a generalist VLA policy, and an event-driven embodied agent, as summarized in~ . The data foundation combines 147 million vision--language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. The vision--language corpus provides general visual-semantic knowledge together with embodied supervision for grounding, scene understanding, affordance prediction, and task reasoning. The robot corpus comprises three complementary components: RoboDesk, a curated collection of open-source real-robot trajectories totaling 3,235 hours; 7,530 hours of licensed real-robot data spanning seven robot configurations; and 4,295 hours of open simulation data. The complete corpus is processed through temporal and visual filtering, kinematic-consistency checks, cross-embodiment action canonicalization, and hierarchical task alignment. RoboDesk and the simulation data broaden task, environment, and embodiment coverage, while the licensed real-robot data provide task-focused manipulation experience. Building on this aligned data foundation, the MR0 policy follows a three-stage training recipe that separates the acquisition of broad action priors from continuous-control learning and real-world adaptation. A shared multimodal backbone is first paired with a discrete action head and pre-trained jointly on vision-language data and tokenized robot actions. Continuous mid-training then introduces an MMDiT~ esser2024mmdit action head and optimizes flow matching over a unified end-effector representation, transferring the pre-trained features to fine-grained control across single-arm and bimanual embodiments. Real-world post-training~ li2026simplevla,li2025vla,ye2025vla starts with supervised finetuning on successful demonstrations. HG-DAgger~ kelly2019hgdagger adds human corrections from policy-induced error states, while RECAP (RL with Experience and Corrections via Advantage-conditioned Policies)~ amin2025pi06star derives advantage labels from outcome-labeled autonomous rollouts. We further introduce Rollback, a collection mechanism that returns to a historical anchor to collect a human replacement while retaining the original policy segment. These paired segments supply direct positive and negative labels to CFG-DAgger and remove the need for value learning and advantage labeling. At deployment, asynchronous action-chunk merging integrates new predictions with commands already being executed, maintaining smooth control without blocking on policy inference. The VLA policy does not explicitly maintain task state across subtasks. MR0 therefore adds an event-driven embodied agent~ huo2026abot,li2026roboclaw,zhang2026harness to retain relevant context, track task progress, and revise plans as conditions change. A Monitor summarizes short visual windows into task-relevant events, and a Memory Manager consolidates these events into a persistent record of task progress and environmental conditions. The Planner updates the active subtask only when a new event changes task progress, reveals a failure, or alters whether the current objective is feasible. Motor execution consequently remains with the VLA policy, while the Planner is invoked only when task-level reassessment is needed. This separation enables the system to retrieve information acquired in earlier tasks, suspend an objective whose prerequisites are temporarily unavailable, and resume it after the required conditions are restored. We evaluate the policy and agent under protocols matched to their respective roles. MR0 achieves 93.6 average success on RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin2 . On RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo , the history-augmented policy ranks fifth in the VLA track by average success rate. With approximately 13.6k hours of embodied training data, MR0 achieves competitive performance across the evaluated manipulation capabilities. Human-intervention data improve both MR0 and across three real-robot tasks. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than across the three tasks. In a separate comparison on Ethernet insertion, MR0 trained with CFG-DAgger reaches 70 success and a progress score of 0.90, outperforming HG-DAgger and RECAP on the same Rollback data. Qualitative agent deployments further illustrate cross-task event retrieval and task resumption following temporary interruptions. Together, these evaluations show how aligned data, continuous policy learning, real-world post-training, and event-level memory address complementary requirements of general-purpose desktop manipulation. title: Towards Label-Efficient Geospatial Foundation Model Adaptation via Positive-Unlabeled Learning for Building Damage Mapping
summary: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.

Geospatial foundation model Weakly supervised learning Disaster response Building damage mapping Remote sensing Introduction Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific model development toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence~ 10916803,11097335 . Advances in model architectures and large-scale pretraining enable GFMs to learn generalizable geospatial representations from vast Earth observation data, providing a transferable foundation for downstream tasks without requiring each task to be learned from scratch~ 10504785,brown2025alphaearth,danish2026terrafm,Feng_2026_CVPR,Herzog_2026_CVPR,FANG2026115256 . However, pretrained GFMs rarely realize their full potential without downstream adaptation~ 11119145,11097335,CHENG2026115694,LI2026115234,LI2026115138,TIAN2025114775 . In this context, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has emerged as an attractive alternative for adapting pretrained GFMs to downstream tasks~ 11119145 . Among the applications that stand to benefit from this shift, mapping the damage to buildings is arguably one of the most consequential and demanding~ rs17101664,ZHENG2025114979,li2026smarttransferleveragingvision,ZHENG2024114416 . Timely, accurate, and large-scale information on damaged buildings is critical for emergency decision-making, response prioritization, post-disaster loss estimation~ GE2023105,ZHENG2025114979,ZHENG2021112636 , and, more broadly, disaster-resilience objectives reflected in the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal 11~ un_sdg_2015 . GFMs are particularly promising in this context because their pretrained representations capture rich geospatial features. However, parameter-efficient adaptation is not necessarily label-efficient. Most existing PEFT approaches rely on fully supervised learning, implicitly assuming the availability of reliable annotations at scale~ 10485462,11533530,11511776 . This assumption is difficult to satisfy in post-disaster operations, when actionable information is needed rapidly while high-quality large-scale annotations remain costly and time-consuming to acquire. This mismatch highlights a fundamental challenge in realizing the full potential of pretrained GFMs for general-purpose geospatial intelligence: achieving not only parameter-efficient adaptation but also label-efficient utilization of pretrained geospatial representations under severely limited supervision. Integrating weakly supervised learning with PEFT offers a promising pathway toward label-efficient adaptation of GFMs. Weakly supervised learning enables models to learn from incomplete, inexact, or inaccurate supervision~ 10.1093/nsr/nwx106,8735810,https://doi.org/10.1049/cit2.12216 . Among various weakly supervised learning paradigms, positive-unlabeled (PU) learning~ PIIROINEN2018119,ZHAO2022328,Zhao_2023_ICCV,10174705,zhao2026noisypair is particularly well aligned with real-world disaster response workflows. In practical disaster response scenarios, obtaining comprehensive damage annotations for both damaged and undamaged buildings at scale is often prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, whereas a limited number of damaged buildings can typically be identified through field surveys, crowdsourced reports, or rapid visual interpretation. Consequently, the available training data often consist of a small set of confirmed damaged buildings (positive samples) and a large pool of unlabeled buildings with unknown damage status. This setting naturally corresponds to PU learning, which aims to train a binary classifier using only positive and unlabeled data. By eliminating the need for exhaustive negative annotations while exploiting abundant unlabeled data, PU learning provides a practical formulation for large-scale mapping of building damage under severe time and resource constraints. Accordingly, developing positive-unlabeled PEFT represents an important step toward efficiently adapting GFMs under weak supervision for operational post-disaster response. In recent years, PU learning has been conceptualized and developed from multiple perspectives. Early studies primarily relied on two-step heuristic methods~ gong2018margin , which first identify reliable negative samples and subsequently train a binary classifier; however, their performance largely depends on the quality of the selected negatives. More recent studies have explored cost-sensitive learning~ 9201373 , label disambiguation~ ijcai2019p590,zhao2026noisypair , density-ratio estimation~ kato2018learning , variational optimization~ NEURIPS2020_aa0d2a80,Zhao_2023_ICCV , and other one-step formulations~ xinrui2023beyond,zhou2025weaklysupervised that jointly leverage positive samples and the entire unlabeled dataset. Among these approaches, risk-estimation-based methods~ kiryo2017positive,ZHAO2022328 have emerged as a prominent paradigm due to their solid theoretical foundations and competitive empirical performance. Despite these advances, the effective integration of PU learning with PEFT for large pretrained GFMs remains largely underexplored. Focusing on label-efficient GFM adaptation, we identify the joint learning of discriminative representations and an accurate decision boundary as a key bottleneck in positive-unlabeled PEFT (Figure~ fig:representation_overlap ). As illustrated in Figure~ fig:representation_overlap ( ), directly combining a PU learning method with PEFT can result in substantial overlap between the learned representations of damaged and undamaged buildings, thereby weakening class separability and limiting subsequent decision-boundary learning. This difficulty is particularly important for PEFT because only a restricted subset of parameters is updated, making effective representation adaptation under weak supervision nontrivial. Moreover, many PU learning methods~ 10264106,pmlr-v235-li24p,10870373 rely on the class prior ( ), i.e., the proportion of positive samples in the underlying data distribution, which must be estimated in advance using separate methods. In the mapping of building damage, this prior corresponds to the proportion of damaged buildings among all buildings. Reliable estimation of is therefore difficult in rapidly evolving post-disaster scenarios, and estimation errors can further degrade classification performance. To enable effective PEFT of GFMs under weak supervision, this study proposes PUMA, a positive-unlabeled geospatial foundation model adaptation framework. Inspired by recent advances in self-supervised and fully supervised representation learning~ BYOL,khosla2020supervised,9578004,lu2023fmicl , the non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement (NeWER) module is introduced to address the challenge of incorrect pairwise relations introduced when representation learning is incorporated into weakly supervised PEFT. Specifically, weak supervision may induce inter-class noisy pairs, which incorrectly pull samples from different classes closer in the embedding space, and intra-class noisy pairs, which erroneously push samples from the same class apart. To counteract these effects, a non-contrastive representation learning architecture is adapted to mitigate the impact of intra-class noisy pairs, while two representation refinement losses ( and ) are proposed to mitigate the impact of inter-class noisy pairs, with the robustness of both losses explained through gradient-based analysis. Building upon the discriminative representations learned by NeWER, the latent-state-based label disambiguation (LaTTE) module is introduced to progressively refine supervision through reversible label disambiguation, enabling PUMA to learn accurate decision boundaries without requiring class prior estimation. Notably, NeWER and LaTTE mutually reinforce each other, and their interaction admits a generalized expectation-maximization (GEM) interpretation that is consistently supported by the experimental results. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and practical potential of PUMA for accurate large-scale damage mapping under highly limited supervision. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:area_data introduces the study areas and datasets used in this study. Section~ sec:method presents the proposed methodology, including the overall PUMA framework and its key components. Section~ sec:EM provides a theoretical analysis of PUMA from a GEM-inspired perspective. Section~ sec:experiments reports and discusses the experimental results, and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper. Study areas and datasets sec:area_data In this study, the performance of PUMA was evaluated from two complementary perspectives: evaluation on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world and local-scale real-world validation. For benchmark evaluation, experiments were conducted on the xView2 Building Damage Assessment (xBD) dataset~ Gupta_2019_CVPR_Workshops and the AIST Building Change Detection (ABCD) dataset~ 7986759 . title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://ai4ce.github.io/VICTR/
summary: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture. We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress. By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training. VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $π_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation. On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%. Project page with code, data and videos: Introduction sec:intro In-context learning (ICL) enables robot policies to adapt their behavior from demonstrations supplied as context, without repeatedly fine-tuning parameters for new tasks at deployment – mirroring large language models, which can infer new tasks from examples in their context without updating model parameters brown2020language . The emergence of this capability in large pretrained models motivates an analogous question for robotics: whether generalist policies can similarly adapt their behavior from demonstrations supplied at inference time. This form of adaptation can potentially address a persistent challenge for robotics foundation models. Despite substantial progress through training on diverse datasets~ pi05 and reinforcement learning~ pi06 , reliable out-of-the-box performance across diverse tasks and environments remains challenging~ roboarena,fang2025intention . Adapting a policy to a new domain often requires additional demonstration collection and fine-tuning, leading to a recurring cost as deployment requirements change. Recent industry systems have begun to demonstrate the promise of ICL, either as an emergent capability of large-scale pretraining~ generalist2026gen15 or through pretraining objectives that explicitly use demonstration videos to specify tasks~ skild2026s1 . Alongside these advances, RICL~ ricl demonstrates that pretrained VLAs can acquire ICL capabilities through retrieval-based post-training without retraining from scratch with extensive resources, learning to generate actions in-context conditioned on selected demonstration chunks. Retrieval-based ICL relies on selecting demonstration chunks that provide useful guidance for the robot's next action. Existing retrieval methods rely on visual similarity~ ricl,mimicdroid , but visually similar observations often occur at different execution stages, making appearance an ambiguous selection signal. We argue that task-relative progress provides an important retrieval signal beyond visual similarity, aligning the current observation with demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution. A related notion appears in RECAP~ pi06 , whose value function estimator (VFE) predicts the negative number of steps remaining until success as a distribution over discretised bins, and forms advantages from it for reinforcement learning. Normalised by the episode horizon, that value runs from at the start of an episode to at success---the scale on which we define task-relative progress, a unitless quantity in comparable across tasks of different lengths. We keep RECAP's formulation and this support, but supervise it with semantic progress annotations rather than elapsed time, and use the estimate to retrieve demonstration chunks at inference rather than to optimise the policy. However, RECAP is conditioned on the current observation and language instruction without a reference demonstration, meaning that adaptation to new tasks depends on the VFE’s prior knowledge of the new language instruction. We seek a progress estimator that can directly use demonstration context to interpret task-specific execution progress, without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. To this end, we make progress estimation itself an in-context learning problem. We introduce an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE) that jointly conditions on the current observation, a language instruction, and a reference demonstration video. The demonstration provides a task-specific reference in-context for the task goal and how it unfolds, supplying execution information beyond the language instruction. IC-VFE uses this reference to assess the current state's progress relative to a demonstrated execution, enabling adaptation through context without task-specific fine-tuning. This estimator forms the core of , our Value-Informed Context Retrieval framework for in-context VLA policies. In , we instantiate IC-VFE with a Gemma-based~ team2025gemma vision-language architecture to predict task-relative progress, and post-train a policy to generate actions conditioned on demonstration chunks retrieved by progress alignment. Both models' weights remain fixed at deployment. In real-world evaluations, IC-VFE agrees with human progress annotations more closely than existing online value estimators on both seen and unseen tasks, and this advantage carries through to control: on unseen out-of-domain tasks, raises the success rate of a fine-tuned baseline from 6.2 to 23.8 and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9 to 55.5 (Figure fig:pull-fig ). In summary, this work makes three primary contributions: An In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE) that uses a reference demonstration video to estimate task-relative progress without task-specific fine-tuning. =-1 VICTR, a -based ICL framework that retrieves demonstration chunks by progress alignment to guide action generation. Real-world evaluations on 8 in-domain and 8 out-of-domain tasks, where progress-informed retrieval raises out-of-domain success from 2.7 for a fine-tuned and 15.0 for a visual-similarity retrieval baseline to 25.0 . Related Work sec:related-work In-context learning for embodied agents. Prior work has explored injecting in-context adaptability into VLAs by retrieving and placing demonstration segments directly in a policy's context window~ ricl,ravla , learning single-demonstration ICL for non-VLA policies via next-token prediction~ icrt , and performing in-context imitation learning with explicit visual reasoning~ iclr . Other work approaches ICL from unstructured human play data~ mimicdroid , studies how retrieved action consequences improve VLA generalization~ reflectivevla , or replaces sequence-conditioned retrieval with explicit correspondence matching between a single demonstration and the current scene~ matchingpolicy . A parallel line of work scales context implicitly by compressing long interaction histories into online-updated fast weights via test-time training~ robottt ; instead keeps policy weights fixed at test time and relies entirely on what is retrieved into the context window. builds most directly on the retrieval-augmented formulation of RICL~ ricl , extending its visual-similarity-only retrieval with an in-context value estimate. Value and reward modeling for VLAs. A growing body of work trains general-purpose value/reward models for robot manipulation, including stage-aware reward modeling~ sarm and other value estimators built on VLM backbones~ robometer,topreward . RECAP~ pi06 shows that a distributional value function trained on episode-level success labels can drive advantage-conditioned policy improvement at scale; our IC-VFE adopts a similar distributional value-bin formulation (Section~ sec:ic-vfe-architecture ) but conditions the prediction on a reference demonstration rather than the query observation alone. Closest in spirit is VITA~ vita , which also targets out-of-domain value calibration but does so by taking online gradient steps on a self-supervised loss at test time; the IC-VFE instead conditions its progress prediction on a reference demonstration, requiring no test-time parameter updates. title: ActPrune: Action-Grounded Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.

Introduction A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop a single policy that can perform diverse manipulation tasks from natural language instructions. Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made progress toward this goal. Many of them build on pretrained vision-language models and generalize to new objects and instructions by inheriting web-scale representations. However, this capability comes with high inference cost. VLA models rely on large vision-language backbones that process hundreds of visual tokens at every control step. In closed-loop control, this computation is repeated for every new observation. As a result, inference latency can limit how fast the robot can respond. Recent methods have explored different ways to reduce the inference cost of VLA models~ robomamba, tinyvla, qail, deervla . Visual token pruning instead reduces computation by removing redundant visual tokens during inference. Existing pruning methods identify redundant tokens from encoded visual features~ divprune, visionzip , attention~ fastv, sparsevlm , temporal changes~ vlacache, specprune , or action information~ vlapruner, specprune . In these approaches, redundancy is mainly determined from the visual observations themselves, after the vision encoder has processed every token. A robot in closed-loop control, however, does not simply observe a sequence of images. Between two observations, the robot executes an action that changes its state and interaction with the scene. The action therefore provides information about where and how the next observation may change. More importantly, this action is already available before the next observation arrives. Unlike visual features or attention scores, it does not require the current observation to be encoded first. The previous action can therefore provide an early signal for identifying visual redundancy before visual encoding. The effect of the action on the observation depends on the camera viewpoint. A standard manipulation setup pairs a fixed third-person camera with a wrist-mounted camera~ droid, libero, vlabench . In the fixed third-person view, the scene stays stable across steps. Change is confined to the region the manipulator occupies. In contrast, the wrist view changes globally and dynamically across steps. These changes arise from camera motion and viewpoint shifts induced by the actions. The action therefore implies contrasting patterns of new information across camera views. Based on these insights, we propose (Fig.~ fig:placeholder ), a training-free framework that exploits the closed-loop structure of robot manipulation to reduce visual computation. Specifically, the action chunk predicted at the previous step is available before the current observation is processed in the visual encoder. It provides a physically grounded prior on where visual computation should be spent without requiring a vision encoder forward pass. leverages this prior to prune visual tokens, projecting the anticipated end-effector trajectory onto the fixed third-person view to mark newly visualized information, while removing motion-compensated redundant patches for the wrist view. The remaining budget is applied after the encoder, where encoder attention ranks the retained tokens. We summarize our contributions as follows: We introduce , a training-free framework that derives geometric priors directly from robot actions, enabling visual token pruning before the vision encoder. We identify that the same action induces distinct redundancy patterns in fixed and wrist-mounted views, and exploit this asymmetry with view-specific pruning. achieves state-of-the-art efficiency on LIBERO~ libero and VLABench~ vlabench , with up to 1.61 speedup and 59.5 FLOPs reduction while preserving competitive performance. However, they require substantial computation at every control step, and inference latency limits the control frequency. Existing approaches improve VLA efficiency at different levels of the inference pipeline. Lightweight architectures~ robomamba, tinyvla replace or compress components of the backbone, quantization methods~ qail reduce the numerical precision of model parameters, and early-exit methods~ deervla terminate computation once intermediate representations suffice. While effective, these methods require retraining or modification of the underlying model. Another line of work targets action generation rather than reducing the cost of individual policy inference. High-frequency VLA frameworks~ openvlaoft, pi0fast increase control frequency through action chunking or asynchronous decoding. By predicting multiple actions at once or decoupling execution from inference, these methods reduce how frequently the full policy must be invoked. However, each policy inference still processes the vision-language backbone, making per-inference visual computation an important bottleneck. Our work is complementary to these approaches. Rather than modifying the policy architecture or action-generation process, we reduce the visual computation required during closed-loop inference without additional training. Visual Token Pruning for VLA Visual token pruning has been widely explored in VLMs to reduce this cost. Existing methods estimate token importance using encoded visual features~ prumerge, visionzip, divprune or language-model attention~ fastv, sparsevlm . Tokens with low estimated importance are then pruned or merged before subsequent transformer layers. This reduces language-model computation by limiting the number of visual tokens. These approaches are effective for static vision-language inputs, but typically determine redundancy from each observation independently. They therefore do not exploit the temporal structure of closed-loop robot control. Recent VLA acceleration methods extend visual token pruning to closed-loop control. Temporal redundancy can be identified from changes across consecutive observations~ vlacache, specprune . Frame differencing provides a lightweight measure of this redundancy, but becomes unreliable under camera motion because it compares pixels at fixed image coordinates. title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under "not X" and "X". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.

Many safety requirements are prohibitions. An operator may forbid contact with a hazardous object or entry into a restricted zone. Such an instruction names no goal. It removes behaviors from the set that the robot may execute, so a robot that executes an excluded behavior violates a safety constraint. Audits show that VLAs under-use language~ zhou2025libero,fei2025libero,fang2026when . A VLA whose actions do not change under a negation or a correction can competently execute a task that the operator excluded. This is an embodied instance of goal misgeneralization~ langosco2021goal,shah2022goal . summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $π_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.

summary: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. As the number of robots grows, however, the communication traffic and the server load become the bottleneck and limit the number of robots that one server can accommodate. In our setting ( on an NVIDIA GB10 without batching), a server accommodates only about two robots when every action chunk is inferred on the server; the number depends on the server but is inversely proportional to the requests per robot. title: ToolDex: An Ego-Exo Human Demonstration Dataset for Creative Physical Tool Use
summary:
Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations.
  We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments.
  Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at https://tooluse-dataset.github.io/.

Introduction Tool use is a fundamental human capability and a key step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence~ goodall1964tool, hunt1996manufacture, shumaker2024animal, fitzgerald2021modeling . In everyday environments, humans do not rely solely on a fixed set of predefined tools; they also flexibly repurpose available objects based on their physical properties and functional affordances. For example, when a knife is unavailable, a person may use a spoon, chopsticks, or another nearby object to divide a cake. This form of creative tool use requires more than recognizing object categories. It demands physical reasoning about contact, geometry and task constraints. As such, physical tool use provides a natural testbed for evaluating whether embodied agents can generalize beyond memorized object-action associations and adapt to novel physical scenarios. Despite recent progress in robotic manipulation black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_05,kim2026cosmos , learning generalizable tool-use behavior remains difficult shi2023robocook, wang2024poco . Task and motion planning methods can solve structured tool-use problems when symbolic task descriptions are carefully specified, but often struggle in open-ended real-world settings~ garrett2021integrated . Recent large language models and vision-language models have shown promising reasoning ability for selecting or describing tools, yet they remain limited in grounding such reasoning into physically executable manipulation~ , liu2024moka,xu2023creative,lin2025robotsmith,gao2025vlmgineer . This gap is especially pronounced in tasks involving deformable target objects (such as sand or cake), non-rigid contacts, and long-horizon interactions, where success depends on fine-grained hand-object-tool dynamics rather than high-level semantic reasoning alone. A major obstacle is the lack of datasets and benchmarks that capture human physical tool-use capabilities at sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing robot tool-use benchmarks are often simulation-based or focus on simplified object interactions, making it difficult to evaluate the complexity of real-world manipulation~ xu2023creative, gao2025vlmgineer,bakhtin2019phyre, zhang2025phystoolbench . Meanwhile, recent egocentric human manipulation datasets have greatly expanded the coverage of hand-object interactions~ hoque2025egodex,punamiya2026egoverse,Li2026egolive,liu2024taco . Among them, TACO explicitly captures tool-action-object compositions for hand-object manipulation~ liu2024taco . However, it does not explicitly model the target objects manipulated by the tools, such as cakes to be cut or water to be stirred. As a result, existing datasets either contain limited tool-use instances or lack the full hand--tool--target-object interactions and annotations needed to study physical tool use. In this paper, we introduce , a large-scale ego-exo human demonstration dataset for learning and benchmarking creative tool-based manipulation ( ). Our dataset is designed around everyday tool-use scenarios in which humans creatively solve manipulation tasks by selecting, adapting, and repurposing available objects. A key feature of our dataset is its explicit coverage of deformable target objects, such as dough, fluids, and sand, where success depends on fine-grained contact and material interactions. To capture these behaviors with high fidelity, we use a synchronized multi-view capture system consisting of two egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras. Egocentric views capture local interaction context, while exocentric views enable accurate multi-view tracking and reconstruction. The resulting dataset provides rich annotations for studying both high-level tool-use reasoning and low-level physical manipulation. Beyond data collection, we use ~to establish a benchmark suite for evaluating tool-use capabilities across three levels. First, we evaluate physical tool-use reasoning, testing whether vision-language models can identify appropriate tools, infer object positions, and provide plausible manipulation strategies. Second, we evaluate 3D and 4D reconstruction, focusing on the recovering hand, tool, and deformable scene states from multi-view observations. Third, we evaluate robot policy learning, where human demonstrations are used to train robot policies for tool-based manipulation. Together, these benchmarks characterize semantic reasoning, spatial perception, and embodied control, offering a comprehensive evaluation protocol for physical tool-use. Our contributions are threefold. First, we present a real-world ego-exo dataset centered on creative physical tool use spanning diverse tools, deformable target objects, tasks, and interaction strategies. Second, we provide rich multi-view annotations that support hand tracking, tool tracking, object interaction analysis, and scene reconstruction. Third, we introduce a benchmark suite that evaluates embodied agents from reasoning to reconstruction to policy execution. We hope this dataset will serve as a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and for developing robots that can creatively use tools in complex, open-world environments. However, they are not designed to systematically capture creative physical tool use in everyday scenarios. They focus on general activities, rigid-object interaction, or affordance modeling and lack detailed hand-tool-target-object interactions, and coverage of deformable objects. ~explicitly targets creative physical tool use and provides data and benchmarks for both high-level reasoning and low-level physical interaction. TACO is closely related to tool-based manipulation, providing a bimanual hand-object interaction dataset with diverse tool--action--object compositions~ liu2024taco . However, it does not model the target objects being acted upon, limiting its ability to capture full tool-use dynamics. Beyond datasets, several benchmarks study physical reasoning and tool use from complementary perspectives. PHYRE evaluates agents on physics-based puzzle solving, emphasizing intuitive reasoning ~ bakhtin2019phyre , while PhysToolBench focuses on tool-use understanding in vision-language models, such as tool selection and strategy explanation~ zhang2025phystoolbench . title: DobotTrack: Target-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Learning for Embodied Person Tracking
summary: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.

Introduction sec:introduction Tracking a person specified in natural language requires an embodied agent to determine whom to track while continually deciding how to move. Unlike tracking in a recorded video, the agent's actions change its viewpoint and the target's visibility, coupling visual recognition with motion generation~ maalouf2023followanything,rspt . Appearance variation, occlusion, and nearby distractors make this coupling particularly important: a plausible trajectory is insufficient if the agent tracks the wrong person. Language-guided embodied tracking therefore calls for representations that connect the referring description, the intended target's image location and the agent's future motion. Vision--language--action models provide a way to learn these capabilities within a shared model. Uni-NaVid unifies several embodied navigation tasks, including person tracking~ zhang2024uninavid , while TrackVLA shares a language-model backbone between target recognition and trajectory planning~ wang2025trackvla . Subsequent work introduces explicit spatial reasoning, target-identification memory, and image-grounded referring decisions~ liu2025trackvlaplusplus,ye2026refertrack . During sustained tracking, changes in illumination and viewpoint can substantially alter the same person's visual appearance, making target association and re-identification after occlusion difficult~ zeng2020illumination,personreid . These variations motivate retaining target-discriminative information across observations. These challenges, illustrated in Fig.~ fig:tracking_overview , raise two complementary questions. First, how can a tracking policy be encouraged to represent the specified target explicitly, rather than relying on trajectory imitation alone? Second, how can historical visual observations be efficiently compressed while preserving target-discriminative appearance cues and scene context essential for reliable person tracking? We address these questions through target-centric perceptual supervision and identity-aware history compression. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded VLA framework built on InternVL3~ internvl3 . We systematically investigate person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification, future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction as auxiliary tasks to improve tracking policy learning. The final model combines mask and box supervision to couple fine-grained foreground delineation with explicit target localization. Building on this grounding, Q-identity compresses historical observations into compact tokens that retain identity-discriminative appearance and spatial context. The language model captures temporal dependencies for trajectory prediction from the chronological sequence of compressed historical and current-frame tokens. The model processes an appearance-based instruction together with a temporal window of RGB observations. The learned mask token and box token precede the waypoint tokens in the causal sequence, allowing the waypoint states to attend to their target-related representations. Task-specific heads decode the resulting hidden states into the target mask, bounding box, and future trajectory in one forward pass. A second consideration is the alignment between policy-learning objectives and real-world annotations. EVT-Bench supports simulated embodied-tracking research~ wang2025trackvla , and TPT-Bench provides robot-egocentric tracking sequences with target boxes and synchronized sensor streams, including odometry~ ye2025tptbench . Complementing these resources, we construct a quadruped-collected dataset with 126 tracking episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated RGB frames. The recordings combine target descriptions, visual observations, and robot motion information. Target masks yield boxes and structured VSC labels, while temporally continuous recordings provide observation histories and future waypoint supervision. Episode-level partitioning keeps samples from the same recorded episode within a single data subset. summary: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. Specialized action models can benefit from this progress by absorbing foundation-model knowledge into their weights and consulting these models during execution. Learning recurring decisions into a compact policy offers efficient control, while access to a capable foundation model can help address unfamiliar failures. The challenge is to combine these routes to sustain coherent behavior throughout an activity. A robot must do more than choose a plausible next action. Each interaction changes the conditions for what follows. A recovered grasp may secure an object in an orientation that prevents its later placement, and a successful local correction may leave the original goal unfinished. Long-horizon autonomy therefore requires reasoning about both the immediate physical state and the consequences of changing it. This motivates our focus on how learned control, task reasoning, and diagnostic evidence cooperate across complete activities, including failures and the attempts to recover from them. Recovery exposes the need to connect task reasoning directly to action generation. Language-guided skill selection and feedback-driven replanning help a robot decide what to attempt next~ saycan,innermonologue,reflect . After a failed grasp, however, choosing to retry does not determine how the next attempt should differ. The controller must adjust its approach, target alignment, or gripper timing using evidence from the failed interaction. Language-conditioned robot policies and vision-language-action (VLA) models learn to map observations and instructions to control~ rt1,rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,grootn1 . title: UAV-Based Computer Vision for Cattle Detection and Feed Bunk Spatial Analysis
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Preprint of paper accepted in IEEE Transactions on AgriFood Electronics
summary: Beef cattle production is central to Brazilian agribusiness and faces growing demands for efficiency, sustainability, and animal welfare. Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) offers tools to address these challenges, particularly through monitoring feeding-related spatial patterns in confined systems. Feeding management plays a decisive role in animal performance, yet its evaluation still relies largely on subjective, labor-intensive visual inspections that are hard to scale and prone to bias. This work proposes a computer vision framework based on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to quantify cattle alignment and spatial dispersion at the feed bunk under real-world feedlot conditions. A UAV dataset was collected during flight campaigns at a commercial feedlot in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. Images were manually annotated into cattle head and cattle back classes to support object detection and image-level spatial analysis of cattle distribution. You Only Look Once (YOLO) models, namely YOLOv8 and YOLOv11, were evaluated, with YOLOv8 small used for the downstream spatial analysis. The feed bunk region was segmented using the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and geometric metrics based on detected head positions were developed to characterize alignment, spacing regularity, and clustering. The selected detector achieved 84.30% mAP50 and 35.50% mAP50-95, with an inference time of approximately 2.7 ms per image on an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti GPU. The resulting metrics distinguished representative regular and irregular spatial distributions by Root Mean Square Deviation - RMSD (1.06 m and 4.26 m), Coefficient of Variation - CV (42.70% and 96.31%), and clustering (0 and 2 clusters), respectively. These findings indicate that the proposed approach can provide indicators for assessing feed bunk spatial patterns in PLF.

Computer Vision, Precision Livestock Farming, UAVs, YOLO, Object Detection, Deep Learning, Cattle Introduction Beef cattle production is central to Brazilian agribusiness and the global meat supply chain. Brazil ranks among the world's largest beef exporters, accounting for nearly 21 of global exports and an estimated herd of 194 million animals in 2024, while generating millions of direct and indirect jobs ani14162340 . In response to increasing global food demand and the need for sustainable intensification, livestock systems in Brazil have progressively incorporated digital technologies, artificial intelligence, and remote sensing tools to improve production efficiency, environmental sustainability, and animal welfare. Traditional cattle monitoring remains a labor-intensive activity that demands time, specialized personnel, and substantial operational costs, particularly in extensive and confined production systems. In this context, Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) has emerged as a modern and strategic approach to livestock management. As defined by 10.2527/af.2017.0102 , PLF extends the principles of precision agriculture to animal production by enabling repeated and individualized monitoring~ MHAFF2025 , with the objective of optimizing animal performance, improving resource efficiency, and reducing environmental impacts. Advances in sensing and data acquisition technologies have enabled the collection of large volumes of behavioral and physiological data~ YUAN2026101867 , supporting more accurate and timely management decisions~ RAJAGUKGUK2025101539 . Among the technologies driving this transition, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become increasingly popular due to their ability to rapidly acquire high-resolution images over large areas at relatively low operational expenses barbedo2018perspectives, barbedo2019review . When combined with computer vision and Deep Learning (DL), UAV imagery offers a powerful platform for key livestock management tasks, such as automated counting, weight estimation, and monitoring feeding-related spatial indicators 10.1093/af/vfae028, eniac , while reducing subjectivity and improving the reliability of zootechnical indicators~ XU2024103732, fi17090431 . In this work, we use a UAV-based dataset collected in a real-world feedlot experiment conducted by the UFGD research group at Campanário Farm, located in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. The imagery was acquired across repeated flight campaigns, providing consistent overhead views. We manually annotated two complementary classes, cattle head and cattle back, to support both effective detection and a more interpretable analysis of animal orientation and spatial distribution at the feed bunk. In this study, feeding-related spatial indicators refer to image-level, instantaneous descriptors of cattle positions relative to the feed bunk, rather than temporal behavioral measurements such as visit frequency, feeding duration, or individual intake. Detecting the cattle head as a distinct class is a choice motivated by its relevance to feeding-related spatial interpretation. Head localization provides evidence of animal orientation relative to the feed bunk and proximity to it, while back detections support future applications such as individual identification. This dataset enables evaluation of detection performance and feed bunk alignment metrics under realistic operational constraints. Feeding management is a key determinant of animal performance in confined systems, and linear feed bunk space plays a central role in shaping competitive interactions among animals. Insufficient feed bunk space intensifies competition, letting dominant animals restrict access and increasing variability in intake and weight gain devries2019feeding , while inadequate management can cause chronic underfeeding (limiting weight gain) or overfeeding (raising waste and ruminal acidosis risk) pritchard2003bunkManagement . Therefore, accurate monitoring of feeding-related spatial distribution along the feed bunk is essential for optimizing nutritional management and ensuring animal welfare. Recent computer vision approaches have also explored automated monitoring of feed bunks, including individual animal identification and feed bunk condition scoring using overhead cameras and clustering techniques, demonstrating the potential of systems to support feeding management decisions~ skae234.002 . Within this context, computer vision offers a promising alternative for evaluating cattle alignment and spatial patterns during observed feeding moments~ CHELOTTI2024150 . UAV imagery enables non-invasive, wide-area observation, allowing quantitative assessment of how animals distribute themselves around the feed bunk. This study combines deep learning based object detection with geometric analysis of cattle spatial arrangement. Detectors from the You Only Look Once (YOLO) family~ make5040083 , specifically YOLOv8 and YOLOv11~ khanam2024yolov11 in configurations ranging from nano to extra large, are evaluated for cattle detection in aerial images. A feed bunk segmentation module defines a precise region of interest for more accurate alignment analysis, and geometric dispersion and uniformity metrics are then computed from the detected positions to support a data-driven evaluation of instantaneous feed bunk spatial patterns. The objective is to propose a computer vision approach using UAV imagery to detect cattle and quantify their spatial dispersion and feeding alignment through YOLO-based models and geometric metrics. The novelty of this work lies in a practical framework that converts standard computer vision outputs into physical, task-specific geometric indicators for instantaneous assessment of cattle distribution along the feed bunk. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: A UAV-based computer vision framework for non-invasive and image-level assessment of cattle spatial distribution at the feed bunk in UAV imagery. A comparative evaluation of multiple YOLO-based object detectors (YOLOv8 and YOLOv11, across model sizes) applied to cattle detection under real farm conditions. A feed bunk segmentation module that defines a precise region of interest for analyzing cattle alignment and spatial distribution at the feed bunk. The development of geometric dispersion and uniformity metrics to quantify cattle distribution along the feed bunk, supporting data-driven monitoring of feed bunk occupation. Experimental evidence that the proposed metrics quantify and discriminate contrasting spatial occupation patterns at the feed bunk, providing a basis for future decision-support tools in feeding management. Section~ sec:relatedWork reviews related work on UAV-based livestock monitoring, YOLO-based cattle detection, segmentation models, and feed bunk analysis. Section~ sec:methods describes the proposed methodology, including the dataset preparation, the training and comparison of YOLO detectors, the feed bunk segmentation procedure, and the geometric metrics used to quantify cattle alignment and dispersion. Section~ sec:experimental-evaluation reports the experimental results, covering both effectiveness and inference time analyses and the evaluation of instantaneous feed bunk spatial patterns using the proposed metrics. Finally, Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work. In feedlot systems, this is particularly relevant because feeding space, bunk design, and competitive interactions influence feeding behavior, intake variation, and animal welfare~ pritchard2003bunkManagement,devries2019feeding . UAV imagery has emerged as a scalable and non-invasive alternative for livestock monitoring, enabling cattle detection, counting, trough reading, production monitoring, and growth assessment under practical farm conditions~ barbedo2020counting,bastos2024drones,wang2025uavlidar,yan2026morphology . However, most UAV-based studies focus on detection, counting, or morphometric analysis~ bhujel2025 , while the geometric relationship between cattle positions and the feed bunk during feeding events remains less explored. YOLO-based detectors have been widely used in agricultural and livestock applications due to their balance between detection accuracy and inference speed~ badgujar2024yoloAgriculture , including cattle body detection and feeding-activity recognition~ qiao2023yolov5asff,guarnidolopez2024yolo . Unlike studies that use detection or segmentation as final outputs, this work uses cattle-back and cattle-head detections and feed bunk segmentation as geometric references for downstream spatial analysis. title: Task-Driven Closed-Loop Design Optimization of Passively Morphing Quadrotors for Contact-Mediated Narrow Gap Traversal
summary: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.

Introduction The width of an aerial robot can impose a hard limit on the environments it can access. In cluttered indoor, industrial, and natural settings, an otherwise traversable route may contain openings narrower than the vehicle's nominal width. Rigid quadrotors can reduce their projected cross-section through aggressive attitude maneuvers~ falangagap,loianno , but the opening must still exceed the vehicle's minimum projected dimension. Moreover, successful traversal requires accurate perception, state estimation, and timing, making this strategy difficult to deploy reliably in real-world settings. Morphing aerial robots can overcome this geometric limitation by temporarily reducing their width. For instance, actuated morphologies~ quadmorphing,foldable,dragon can decrease width on demand, but increase system complexity through additional servomotors and adaptive control strategies. Thrust-triggered quadrotor arm folding through passive joints~ bucki2019,bucki2023 can achieve large and rapid shape changes, but requires invertible thrust and limiting maneuverability to avoid unintentionally triggering the passive joints. Contact-mediated passively reconfigurable designs are therefore particularly attractive as they leverage contact with the environment to initiate and maintain shape change~ squeeze,morphy,girardi2025bioinspired,fabris2021soft,fabris2022crash without requiring additional actuators or invertible thrust. However, the geometry and compliance of these existing designs are not specifically optimized for the traversal task, where the trade-off between in-flight rigidity (and consequently tracking accuracy and power consumption) and the maximum achievable squeeze is not specifically addressed. Aerial robots that achieve contact-mediated in-flight narrow-gap traversal only pass through gaps up to 29 narrower than the drone's span~ squeeze,morphy,girardi2025bioinspired . A well-designed passively morphing quadrotor must remain effectively rigid under rotor loads during nominal flight and simultaneously easily reduce its width when the opening applies contact forces. After traversal, it must restore the nominal flight configuration. A design that is too flexible can deform during normal flight, leading to worse control, while a stiffer structure can be difficult to compress through the gap. When airframe geometry and compliance are selected by hand, it is particularly difficult to identify which combinations best enable both successful gap traversal and good nominal flight control performance. Previous works show contact-mediated narrow-gap traversal is possible but generally propose a planar quadrotor architecture and compliance guided by engineering intuition. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has jointly optimized airframe geometry and compliance directly driven by closed-loop performance over the complete narrow-gap traversal and recovery task. In this work, we introduce a task-driven closed-loop design optimization approach for soft quadrotors, optimized for narrow-gap traversal. Figure~ fig:overview summarizes the proposed closed-loop design optimization pipeline and the resulting vehicle's key capabilities. We jointly optimize a 22-parameter quadrotor geometry and the programmable nonlinear torque deflection response of two passively folding side arms directly for traversal success. summary: Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physicallygrounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations.
