Introduction When tightening a screw or mating a nut, vision alone is often insufficient: successful execution depends on subtle contact cues, force feedback, and proprioceptive information. In order to perform such tasks, it would also be useful to anticipate how the robot's actions affect the world, such as how contact will form, how an object will move, and how force will propagate. This motivates robot models that jointly reason about actions and their consequences. World-action models (WAMs)~ cheang2024gr,li2025unified,won2025dual,wu2024unleashing,hu2024video,kim2026cosmos,liang2025video,pai2025mimic,zhu2025unified, huang2025unified address this by jointly modeling future observations and actions within a single generative model. Recent work~ li2025unified,zhu2025unified,huang2025unified shows that such auxiliary dynamics learning can improve model capability and generalization in robot control. However, existing WAMs still have two key limitations for robot manipulation. First, most prior WAMs are built primarily around visual observations, leaving tactile and force information largely unexplored. Second, these models typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders, often trained with pixel reconstruction or self-supervised visual objectives. While such encoders provide useful features for image generation or semantic understanding, their representations are not necessarily aligned with robot control. This issue is even more pronounced for tactile, where broadly-applicable pretrained encoders are less established. A natural solution is to finetune the encoders end-to-end with the WAM objective, but we find that naive finetuning leads to feature collapse: the encoder and diffusion backbone co-adapt to produce latents that are easy to denoise but less useful for control. To address the above limitations, we present MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns task-relevant representations end-to-end with a latent diffusion backbone. We build on Multimodal Diffusion Forcing (MDF)~ huang2025unified , but instead of modeling dynamics in a frozen latent space, MDF++ finetunes observation encoders jointly with the world-action model under a mixture of task-oriented objectives, including policy learning, joint action--observation prediction, forward dynamics modeling, and inverse dynamics modeling. To avoid feature collapse during joint training, MDF++ introduces a cross-modal training strategy with selective gradient back-propagation, which encourages the latent space to capture the interplay between different modalities, yielding representations that are better aligned with robot control. Our key contributions are three-fold. First, we propose MDF++, a diffusion-based visuo-tactile WAM that learns task-relevant multimodal representations end-to-end using cross-modal prediction. Second, we introduce a selective gradient-flow strategy that enables stable joint training of observation encoders and the world-action model while avoiding feature collapse. Third, we evaluate MDF++ on seven contact-rich manipulation tasks, including two real-world threading tasks requiring millimeter-level precision. In simulation, MDF++ outperforms frozen-encoder baselines by 28 and naive joint training by 22 . In real, it outperforms video-based WAMs~ zhu2025unified by 29 . Related Work World modeling for Robotics Recently, world models have shown great promise for robotics. One line of work studies action-conditioned world models (WAs) to predict the future outcomes of actions, enabling data generation~ team2025gigabrain, wang2026interactive , planning~ du2024video,zhou2024dino,maes2026leworldmodel,assran2025v , and policy evaluation~ team2025evaluating, wang2026interactive, zhang2025real . Another line of work, world action models (WAMs), jointly predicts future observations and actions~ cheang2024gr,li2025unified,won2025dual,wu2024unleashing,hu2024video,kim2026cosmos,liang2025video,pai2025mimic,zhu2025unified, huang2025unified, zheng2026omnivta . However, most prior work is limited to vision, whereas MDF++ captures the dynamics of multimodal sequences including tactile, force and robot proprioception. Beyond the choice of modalities, a key design question is how to obtain the representation space in which world-action dynamics are learned. Most existing WA and WAMs rely on frozen pretrained encoders, typically trained with pixel reconstruction~ podell2024sdxl or self-supervised learning objectives~ oquab2023dinov2, assran2023self . For example, UWM~ zhu2025unified and UVA~ li2025unified use pretrained image VAEs~ rombach2022high,podell2024sdxl , Dino-WM~ zhou2024dino predicts future states in the DINO feature space~ oquab2023dinov2 , and MDF~ huang2025unified builds on a diffusion-based point-cloud VAE~ luo2021diffusion . While these encoders provide useful features for visual generation or semantic understanding, they are not necessarily aligned with robot control. As a result, the world model may learn dynamics in a representation space that is suboptimal for manipulation. In contrast, MDF++ starts from a pretrained encoder and finetunes it end-to-end with the latent world-action model backbone. Through cross-modal supervision from tactile, force, and actions, MDF++ learns a representation space that is better suited for robot manipulation. FLARE~ zheng2025flare finetunes the encoder using an EMA target, but it is not designed for unified WAMs with multiple query distributions and also does not support multimodal reasoning. Multimodal Representation learning for Manipulation The integration of multi-sensory information, such as audio~ du2022play, li2022see,liu2024maniwav , force~ noseworthy2025forge, kang2025robotic, wu2024tacdiffusion , is critical for robot control. Particularly, there is growing interest in combining vision and tactile for adaptive and precise manipulation. Much of the prior works learn a visuo-tactile policy using either imitation learning~ huang20243d,george2025vital, liu2025vitamin, xu2025unit, zhu2026touch or reinforcement learning~ van2016stable, suresh2024neuralfeels, lee2019making, chen2022visuo, hansen2022visuotactile, yuan2024robot, sferrazza2024power , where representations are primarily supervised by action prediction or task reward. Other works study self-supervised tactile~ cao2023learn, higuera2024sparsh, zhao2024transferable,xu2025unit or visuo-tactile representation learning~ dave2024multimodal,zhu2026touch . In contrast, our work studies representation learning for multimodal world-action models. While these models provide richer supervision through action and cross-modal prediction, naively training encoders with diffusion losses can cause feature collapse. We address this with selective gradient flow and show that the proposed method outperforms policy-only training and pretrained self-supervised encoders~ higuera2024sparsh . Given a clean sample , the forward process produces a noisy sample at diffusion step , where and is determined by a noise schedule. The reverse model is trained to denoise by predicting the injected noise, yielding the standard objective . At inference time, samples are generated by iterative denoising from Gaussian noise. Latent diffusion models perform this denoising process in a learned latent space rather than directly in the input space~ rombach2022high . summary: A language model can repair a robot policy's lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows. We bring weight-space programming to robot foundation policies: GPT-6 Astra reads weights and uses a CPU workspace and budgeted simulator feedback, without gradient updates or new demonstrations. Three independent sessions on $π_{0.5}$ all improve success on 765 held-out paraphrases; the best raises success from 86.3\% to 92.0\% (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired $p=1.31\times10^{-10}$). Among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens, success rises from 74.3\% to 87.5\%; the other 430 episodes have zero outcome changes. Matched random-direction edits do not help. Full replacement using the editor's own lexicon explains much of the gain but produces more regressions; its direct difference from the editor is not significant at 0.05. Across 13 further robot sessions, the editor declines 12 candidates; the sole retained edit does not show a significant held-out gain. Separately, benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0\% to 48.6\%, while the evaluated VLA's aggregate rate is unchanged. Introduction A language model can repair some robot-policy failures by changing a few rows of the policy's weights. Our strongest result changes 65 token-embedding rows: success rises from 74.3 to 87.5 on 335 held-out instructions containing an edited token, with no outcome changes on the other 430 instructions. The manipulation skill is already available; the edit changes which language reaches it. Consider a policy that turns on the stove under its canonical instruction, but picks up a plate when asked to ``activate the cooking appliances heat source'' (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Both actions are familiar tasks in the same scene. The failure is a mismatch between wording and the task represented by the policy, rather than the absence of a stove-turning behavior. A camera perturbation or a dropped object presents a different debugging problem: changing the interpretation of a word may not supply the required visual or recovery behavior. Takehi et al.~ wsp introduced weight-space programming: a general-purpose LLM inspects and changes another network's parameters directly, without gradient optimization. Their demonstrations span games and language models, and motivate a distinction between removing an obstacle to an existing ability and creating a new ability. We bring this experimental setup to robot foundation policies. We test both whether an editor can find a useful intervention and whether it declines interventions that fail its own checks. GPT-6 Astra receives policy weights, a persistent CPU Python workspace, and a budgeted forward tool. It can inspect tensors and write replacements, but cannot train the policy or change the deployment program. title: Lightweight Path-Aware Frontier Re-ranking for LiDAR-Based UAV Exploration
comment: Accepted for presentation at RIVF 2026 (20th International Conference on Computing and Communication Technologies)
summary: Autonomous 3D exploration with UAVs requires efficient target selection under limited flight time and onboard computation. In conventional Euclidean-distance-based frontier pipelines, geometric distance may poorly represent the actual collision-free travel cost in cluttered environments, leading to inefficient frontier choices. This paper presents a lightweight path-aware frontier re-ranking method for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. The method first retains a small top-N set of promising frontier candidates using a lightweight utility function and then applies time-bounded RRT* planning to estimate their feasible path costs for re-ranking. The path generated for the selected frontier is further reused for navigation to reduce redundant global planning. Experiments in three warehouse-like environments show that the proposed method consistently produces shorter exploration trajectories than conventional frontier baselines, with traveled-distance reductions of up to 14.1%, while reducing exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments and remaining competitive in the third. The method maintains map detail comparable to the conventional OctoMap-based baseline, demonstrating an effective trade-off between exploration efficiency and mapping quality.

INTRODUCTION sec:introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have attracted increasing attention for autonomous exploration due to their high mobility in three-dimensional environments and their ability to access complex or hazardous areas~ huang2024efficient,caiza2024frontiercollector . These properties make UAVs suitable for applications such as search and rescue, infrastructure inspection, environmental monitoring, warehousing, and large-scale 3D mapping~ ye2025autonomous . In these scenarios, autonomous 3D exploration enables a UAV to incrementally acquire information about an unknown environment and construct a spatial map for subsequent navigation and decision-making tasks~ huang2024efficient . In a typical autonomous exploration process, the robot repeatedly determines where to move next based on the currently available map. During flight, onboard sensors such as LiDAR and cameras provide measurements that are integrated into a 3D representation for mapping, planning, and navigation~ geng2024epic,canh2026semantic . The planner then identifies informative unexplored regions, selects the next target, and generates a safe trajectory toward it. For UAVs, this process is particularly challenging because exploration must be performed in large three-dimensional spaces under limited flight time and onboard computational resources~ geng2024epic,li2026scope . Existing autonomous exploration approaches can be broadly categorized into sampling-based next-best-view (NBV) methods and frontier-based methods~ liu2025enhancing,lindqvist2024errt . NBV methods sample candidate viewpoints or motion sequences and evaluate their expected information gain, enabling explicit reasoning about visibility and map uncertainty. Several approaches further integrate RRT or RRT to search for informative viewpoints or feasible trajectories in partially known environments~ lindqvist2021exploration,lindqvist2024errt . While effective, evaluating a large number of sampled candidates and trajectories can introduce considerable online computational cost, particularly in large 3D environments~ lindqvist2024errt,huang2024efficient . Frontier-based exploration offers an alternative paradigm by directing the robot toward frontiers, i.e., boundaries between known free space and unknown regions~ yamauchi1997frontier,liu2025enhancing . Existing methods improve different components of this paradigm. Batinovi'c et al.~ batinovic2021multi proposed a multi-resolution frontier-based planner that exploits the octree structure of OctoMap for efficient frontier detection and clustering, while Caiza et al.~ caiza2024frontiercollector introduced a frontier collector strategy that stores, validates, and reuses detected frontiers to improve exploration completeness and safety. Several depth-camera-based UAV exploration frameworks further incorporate more sophisticated planning mechanisms. FUEL~ zhou2021fuel combines incremental frontier structures with hierarchical planning, Dai et al.~ dai2020fast incorporate travel-time-aware evaluation of candidate viewpoints, and SCOPE~ li2026scope employs a skeleton graph with hierarchical on-demand planning. In contrast, EPIC~ geng2024epic is a LiDAR-based framework that directly exploits point-cloud observations and maintains an incremental topological representation for large-scale exploration. These approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of path-, time-, and topology-aware reasoning for autonomous UAV exploration. Nevertheless, conventional frontier-based pipelines that select targets using Euclidean distance and information gain can still underestimate the travel cost of navigating around obstacles. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:problem , a geometrically close frontier may require a long collision-free detour, while a more distant frontier may be reachable via a shorter path. Although path-aware and time-aware exploration have been investigated in previous work, incorporating feasible path estimates into a conventional frontier-selection pipeline raises a practical trade-off: planning for more candidates can improve the travel-cost estimate but increases computational effort. Evaluating every detected frontier with a sampling-based planner is therefore not always desirable. To address this trade-off, we propose a two-stage path-aware frontier re-ranking strategy that augments an existing LiDAR-based frontier exploration pipeline without redesigning its mapping and frontier-generation components. First, candidates are ranked using a low-cost utility based on information gain and Euclidean distance, and only the top- candidates are retained. Second, time-bounded RRT planning estimates feasible path costs for the retained candidates, which are then re-ranked accordingly. The feasible path associated with the selected frontier is also reused for navigation when valid, avoiding an otherwise redundant planning request. The contribution is a bounded, selective use of established planning tools within frontier selection, rather than a new frontier detector or motion planner. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: A two-stage path-aware frontier re-ranking strategy that combines low-cost top- candidate filtering with time-bounded RRT path-cost estimation, restricting expensive path evaluation to a small shortlist. A reusable-path mechanism that forwards the validated path obtained during frontier evaluation to navigation, avoiding a repeated global planning request when possible. An evaluation in three simulated warehouse-like environments, including comparisons with existing exploration systems, a path-reuse ablation, and sensitivity analyses of exploration time, travel distance, and map detail. title: Extended Model-Based Learned Inertial Odometry
summary: Inertial odometry is a compelling approach to state estimation for agile quadrotor flight due to its affordability, low weight, and robustness to perceptual degradation. However, relying only on integrated inertial measurements is impractical, as sensor errors and time-varying biases lead to significant pose drift. Although recent advances have enabled inertial odometry for drone racing, existing approaches show limited generalization to trajectories not seen during training. This work improves generalization by adopting a body-frame representation and incorporating body-frame torque dynamics into the learning pipeline. The learned model predicts short-horizon relative displacements, which are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for quadrotor pose estimation on unseen trajectories. An additional evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets, with whole trajectory shapes held out of training, confirms a lower velocity error on every held-out set and shows that the torque input is most informative when it is derived from the rotor signals. Code, data pipeline and trained models are publicly available.

Accurate state estimation is essential for enabling this autonomy. Inertial odometry (IO) is a promising state-estimation approach in resource-constrained systems because of its low computational and storage requirements. Moreover, IO is not affected by common visual-odometry failure modes such as motion blur, low-texture environments, and high-dynamic-range scenes. These conditions are common during agile flight maneuvers, where dedicated visual processing is often required~ kuruppu2024robust . Although 6-DoF poses can be estimated by integrating inertial measurements, commodity IMUs suffer from bias drift, noise, scale-factor errors, misalignment, and vibration-induced inaccuracies, which cause long-term estimation drift yang2020online . If reliable pose estimation can be achieved using only inertial sensing, robots can be made smaller and lighter, improving agility and operating range. Recently, deep learning has enabled progress in inertial odometry for state estimation. For example, liu2020tlio show that motion priors for pedestrians can be learned from IMU measurements, with accuracy comparable to recent visual-inertial odometry (VIO) methods. Unlike pedestrian motion, quadrotor motion lacks a consistent prior that can be learned directly from IMU measurements. However, the quadrotor dynamics model can serve as a motion prior, which can then be corrected using onboard measurements (e.g., IMU data) and control outputs. Cioffi~et al.~ CioffiRal2023 introduced a method that incorporates a quadrotor dynamics model and collective thrust to learn quadrotor translational motion for a given trajectory. The resulting relative position displacements are used to update an EKF propagated from IMU measurements. The method is accurate on known trajectories in the drone-racing context; however, its generalization to unseen trajectories remains unclear. Our work adopts the general framework of Cioffi~et al.~ CioffiRal2023 . We introduce two main modifications to improve its performance: We introduce body-frame torque dynamics into the learned inertial odometry pipeline, enabling the model to account for angular acceleration–induced effects that are otherwise absorbed as unmodeled noise. We reformulate the learning problem in the body frame, improving generalization and observability. We experimentally validate the model by integrating it into a state-of-the-art learning-based inertial odometry framework and comparing it with prior art, on Blackbird and DIDO and on four further public quadrotor datasets with held-out trajectory shapes. The effectiveness of the proposed modifications is demonstrated on several widely used offline datasets, and the new model is deployed on a real drone. RELATED WORK Odometry, the process of estimating a robot's position and orientation over time from its internal sensor data, is important for drones, which often operate indoors, below the GPS canopy, or in urban canyons. Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) is often the preferred choice, since accurate, low-drift pose estimation from visual input is essential for tasks ranging from stable hovering to fast maneuvers in complex environments. The main VIO approaches are filter-based and optimization-based methods. Filter-based methods belong to the multistage constraint Kalman filter (MSCKF) family derived from~ Mourikis-2007-icra . Optimization-based methods, such as OKVIS~ OKVIS and Kimera-VIO~ Kimera , are often found to be more accurate than filtering-based methods. Recently, hybrid filtering-optimization approaches have reported superior accuracy by combining the two approaches~ HybVIO . IMU-only odometry is beneficial over VIO in certain scenarios due to its robustness to visual degradation, lower computational demand, and independence from lighting and environmental conditions. IMU odometry works by measuring acceleration and angular velocity at very high rates, allowing real-time motion estimation even when cameras fail or the environment is visually ambiguous (e.g., darkness, featureless walls, smoke). This makes IMU odometry especially valuable for high-dynamic maneuvers and visually challenging environments as a complementary subsystem or short-term fallback for VIO. Learning inertial odometry can substantially improve IMU-only odometry by addressing its core limitations, most notably sensor drift, non-linearity, and bias sensitivity. Deep learning can be used to estimate velocity and displacement from IMU data. Methods like IONet~ IONet , A2DIO~ A2DIO and NILoc~ NILoc treat inertial navigation as a sequential task by predicting relative motion. These predictions are often integrated into EKF or optimization frameworks. To maintain consistency, many approaches transform IMU data into global coordinates such as a heading-agnostic coordinate frame (HACF)~ RoNIN . title: ODEAction: From Predicting Chunks to Evolving Actions

summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically generate actions in chunks, organizing continuous robot execution into separately predicted segments and thus introducing potential discontinuities at action-chunk transitions. We propose ODEAction, a chunk-free action generation paradigm that replaces action-chunk prediction with Continuous Action Evolution. Given visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioceptive information, ODEAction learns an action transition field defined over action space, where a transition vector characterizes the evolution rate of the current action with respect to evolution time. During execution, the model takes the current action as its initial condition and integrates the learned field using an ordinary differential equation (ODE), recursively generating subsequent actions with explicit dependencies. ODEAction is implemented as an action head and does not depend on a specific vision-language backbone architecture. Experiments on LIBERO, EBench, RoboTwin, and real robots show that ODEAction improves both task performance and trajectory quality over matched action-chunking baselines, with particularly pronounced gains on fine manipulation tasks.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,li2024roboflamingo,ReconVLA-2025,SpatialVLA-2025,RoboVLMs-2024,li2024cogact widely adopt action-chunk generation (Action Chunking Generation): they jointly predict a sequence of future actions in a single inference pass, organizing continuous execution into successively generated action chunks~ black2024pi_0,black2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t,kim2025fine,shukor2025smolvla,PDVLA-2025,wen2025tinyvla . However, adjacent chunks predicted independently typically lack explicit temporal consistency constraints across chunk boundaries, potentially causing abrupt action changes and trajectory discontinuities at transitions~ black2025real,liu2024bidirectional ( (a)). Existing methods alleviate this issue by imposing constraints on continuity across chunks: RTC~ black2025real constrains new action chunks during inference, whereas Training-time RTC~ black2025training and Legato~ liu2026learning introduce continuity constraints during training. Nevertheless, these methods still treat action chunks as the fundamental unit of generation, improving the connections between chunks rather than changing the action generation paradigm. This leads us to ask a further question: can we move beyond chunk-wise prediction and directly model the continuous evolution of actions over time? Robot execution itself progresses incrementally over time rather than occurring in action chunks. We therefore characterize continuous action evolution using an ordinary differential equation (ODE): the current action provides the starting point, a learned action evolution rate determines subsequent changes, and integration progressively generates an action sequence without jointly predicting an entire future action chunk. Action generation thus shifts from predicting future segments to learning the dynamics that drive actions to evolve continuously. From this perspective, we propose ODEAction, an action generation paradigm centered on Continuous Action Evolution. Given visual observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive information, ODEAction learns an Action Transition Field defined over action space. At each action and evolution time, the field outputs a transition vector representing the evolution rate of the current action with respect to evolution time. During training, we construct a target field around demonstration trajectories that combines progression along the demonstrations with deviation correction, and learn this field through direct supervision. During inference, starting from the current action, we integrate the learned action transition field using an ODE, so that each generated action becomes the starting point for subsequent evolution, instead of independently predicting and concatenating action chunks ( (a)). ODEAction is implemented as an action head that can be integrated with different vision-language backbones. We evaluate ODEAction on simulation benchmarks, including LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin , and EBench~ gao2026ebench , as well as on real-robot tasks. Compared with matched action-chunking baselines, ODEAction improves both task performance and action trajectory quality, achieving a 61.8 relative improvement in average success rate on EBench. Further analysis shows that evaluation units exhibiting larger improvements in boundary continuity also tend to achieve greater success-rate gains. In a representative execution of the real-world Place Cup task, ODEAction smoothly transports a water-filled cup without spilling, while producing a more continuous end-effector trajectory ( (a)). Our contributions are threefold: We propose ODEAction, a chunk-free generation paradigm based on continuous action evolution, transforming action generation from future action-chunk prediction into a learnable continuous evolution process. Extensive experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-robot tasks show that ODEAction improves both task performance and trajectory quality over matched action-chunking baselines, with particularly substantial benefits on fine manipulation tasks. We identify a systematic relationship between improvements in trajectory quality and gains in task performance: boundary discontinuity reduction is strongly positively correlated with success-rate gains, and evaluation units with greater improvements in trajectory continuity generally achieve larger task-performance gains. title: SURE:Spatiotemporal Uncertainty Representation for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Learning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data. In manipulation tasks, this dependence is compounded by structured spatiotemporal uncertainty in the action space: multiple nearby actions or trajectories may successfully solve the same task, while semantically equivalent demonstrations often unfold at different speeds. Standard pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target, imposing an unnecessary learning burden under such uncertainty. We present SURE, a data-efficient VLA training framework that explicitly models both spatial and temporal uncertainty. SURE augments a VLA backbone with a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that captures spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins. It further introduces Soft-DTW alignment supervision to accommodate local timing variations between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. Together, these two components reduce sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, enabling more data-efficient action learning. We evaluate SURE on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks. Even with only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, SURE achieves manipulation success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.

As a result, a central question in robot learning is no longer whe\-ther such end-to-end policies can work, but which action-learning paradigm can most efficiently turn expensive robot demonstrations into robust manipulation behaviors. This question is important in practical settings, where collecting real-world robot data remains slow, costly, and inherently noisy. One source of difficulty is the inherent uncertainty in robot action data. Many manipulation tasks admit multiple valid solutions which the end effector can approach from slightly different poses, move at different speeds, or follow different but equally successful trajectories. Importantly, this uncertainty is structured rather than arbitrary. It typically exhibits strong local spatiotemporal correlations, actions that are close to a successful action in action space, or adjacent in time to a successful motion pattern, are often still correct. Treating supervision as a single exact target therefore introduces an unnecessary learning burden. A policy can be semantically correct yet still incur a large penalty simply because its prediction does not match the demonstrator's exact pose or timing. Existing action representations only partially address this issue. Early and widely used VLA decoders often rely on tokenized or autoregressive action prediction brohan2022rt1,kim2024openvla , while recent systems increasingly adopt diffusion- and flow-based action heads to better model multimodal futures chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t . These generative action heads are expressive and have become a popular choice for modern VLAs. However, their flexibility does not automatically yield data efficiency. When supervision still treats each action label as an isolated point, the model must discover from scratch that neighboring actions and slightly shifted trajectories should receive similar credit. In practice, this often means that the policy needs more data before it can internalize the local structure of valid robot behavior. Recent work suggests that structured probabilistic action representations can be more sample-efficient and interpretable than unstructured point prediction. Instead of regressing a single action target, these methods model uncertainty with discretized action spaces, heatmap-like predictions, or voxel-space probability distributions, thereby injecting locality and multimodality into the output space james2021c2f,shridhar2022peract,goyal2023rvt,yang2026actionmap . However, most of this literature focuses primarily on spatial uncertainty, while temporal uncertainty is still typically handled with exact per-step supervision. Temporal uncertainty creates a second challenge. Even for the same task and intent, demonstrations can unfold at different speeds because of operator preferences, hesitation, embodiment dynamics, or minor contact events. Standard framewise regression losses such as L1 or L2 fail to account for this uncertainty and instead penalize timing differences directly. As a result, the model may overfit to demonstrator-specific execution speeds rather than the underlying behavior. This problem is closely related to the alignment problem long studied in speech recognition, where dynamic time warping (DTW) was introduced to compare signals that differ in local speaking rate sakoe1978dtw . Its differentiable variant, Soft-DTW cuturi2017softdtw , offers a natural way to bring this idea into gradient-based policy learning, yet it remains underexplored as a supervision mechanism for action prediction in VLA-style robot policies. In this paper, we tackle both spatial and temporal uncertainty with a simple, data-efficient VLA design, as shown in Figure~ fig:intro_image . We introduce a lightweight probabilistic action decoder built with transposed convolutions that models spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins and can be supervised directly with standard pointwise losses. We further couple this head with Soft-DTW alignment supervision, which aligns action sequences executed at different speeds and accounts for temporal uncertainty across demonstrations. Together, these design choices encourage the policy to learn a distribution over valid behaviors rather than memorize a one-to-one mapping from observations to exact action labels. Empirically, SURE outperforms strong baselines with matched or fewer optimization steps. On LIBERO liu2023libero , our method reaches 97.0 average success after 10k steps, surpassing OpenVLA-OFT trained for 50k steps. With only 25 of the LIBERO-Spatial data, our method also exceeds the full-data baseline. These gains extend to RoboTwin 2.0 chen2025robotwin2 and our real-world benchmark. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that models spatial uncertainty with locally correlated action bins while enabling fast, parallel expectation-based decoding without iterative denoising. Second, we incorporate Soft-DTW alignment supervision to improve robustness to demonstrations with similar task intent but different execution speeds. Third, extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and our real-world benchmark show that our method achieves stronger training and data efficiency than competitive baselines, requiring fewer optimization steps or less training data. More recent work has explored continuous parallel decoding and improved fine-tuning recipes to reduce inference cost and increase adaptation performance kim2025oft,wen2024tinyvla . Another major direction models actions as distributions rather than single point estimates. This includes diffusion- and flow-based action heads for multimodal action generation chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t , as well as structured probabilistic outputs such as discretized spatial bins, heatmaps, and voxel-space distributions james2021c2f,shridhar2022peract,goyal2023rvt,yang2026actionmap . Soft-DTW extends this idea to a differentiable objective, making it suitable for gradient-based learning cuturi2017softdtw . Improving data efficiency remains a core challenge in robot learning because large-scale demonstrations are expensive to collect, especially on real hardware. Existing efforts improve efficiency from several angles: scaling diverse cross-embodiment datasets for transfer oxe2023rtx,ghosh2024octo,kim2024openvla , designing better adaptation and fine-tuning recipes kim2025oft , building smaller or faster VLA architectures wen2024tinyvla , and injecting stronger geometric structure into the action output space james2021c2f,shridhar2022peract,goyal2023rvt,yang2026actionmap . title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

Introduction sec:introduction In nature, manipulation draws on general intelligence. Animals can recruit their memory, reasoning, and problem-solving faculties when interacting with objects, with cognitive processes continuing to shape action as it unfolds~ BirdEmery2009,CisekKalaska2010,Duncan2010 . In robotics, much recent work has focused on models specialized for robot control, including vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), trained or fine-tuned on robot demonstrations~ Brohan2023,Ye2026 . Generalist AI models have also been applied to manipulation, often through skill orchestration or offline program synthesis. In the first setting (skill orchestration), the model selects and sequences low-level skills such as grasping and placing~ Ahn2022,Huang2022,Li2026:RoboClaw . It can revise the plan as new observations arrive, but the available skills limit the generalist model's control authority and the granularity at which it can command the manipulator. Since the generalist model's interactions with the world are mediated by the provided skills, it is constrained by the skills' limitations. In the second setting (offline program synthesis, sometimes known as `code-as-policies'), the model writes a control program before execution~ Liang2023,rho,Shen2026:EmbodiedSWE,harnesspai . The program can incorporate perception and feedback, but the generalist model is not in the loop and cannot reconsider the overall control strategy as the task unfolds. A key obstacle to direct manipulation has been the limited spatial cognition of generalist frontier models~ Ramakrishnan2025 . However, spatial cognition has been advancing~ Chen2026:BabyVision,Zeller2026 , with recent models demonstrating convincing spatial planning, sensorimotor coordination, and embodied fluid intelligence~ Anonymous2026:SpatialCognition,anonymous2026benchmarking . These advances make a third approach increasingly viable: the generalist model remains in the control loop and commands the manipulator directly, revising its actions as the task unfolds~ capx,Hu2026:VIA,Jia2026,yang2026astranomy . We refer to this category as Agentic Manipulation Policies (AMPs). In this paper, we systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies across models and harness configurations. We present , a reference harness that provides visual observations, code execution, and direct control of manipulator motion. Paired with frontier models, achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results on the RoboLab-120~ robolab and CaP-Gym~ capx benchmarks. The agent succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, compared to 49 for FLUX 3 Action~ flux3a and 30 for ~ pi05 , thus reducing the failure rate by 15x and 20x, respectively, relative to these WAM and VLA baselines. See and the supplementary video for curated highlights. We document emergent behaviors that arise as the agent brings its broader cognitive faculties to bear on manipulation. When a book lies flat on a table and cannot be grasped as is, the agent pushes it to the table edge to expose a graspable surface. When a target object is hidden, the agent moves occluding objects out of the way to find it. When a large fruit is too wide to grasp, the agent pins it against a heavier object, slides the gripper underneath, and lifts it like a forklift. Failed actions can themselves supply information: the agent infers an unseen shelf from a blocked motion and changes its grasp and approach. On the real robot, the agent diagnoses camera calibration errors from discrepancies between commanded and observed motion, then compensates for them in subsequent actions. None of these behaviors are specified in the prompt or supplied as skills in the harness. The generalist model develops them within each episode by reasoning about geometry, contact, and the consequences of its own actions. We also investigate few-shot and continual learning from the agent's own experience. We equip with a persistent memory, allowing the agent to record useful observations, strategies, and code after reflecting on its successes and failures. Experience accumulates in this memory bank, while the model's weights remain fixed. No expert demonstrations or gradient updates are required. We evaluate this approach on the 42 bimanual manipulation tasks of RoboDojo~ robodojo . Practicing individual tasks raises the success rate on unseen layouts from 26.4 to 84.1 , above all entries on the benchmark's leaderboard. We also test whether the agent can accumulate knowledge across tasks via continual learning. In this setting, the agent attempts each task once, in sequence, and updates its memory representation in the course of this continual deployment. A single pass through the tasks more than doubles the success rate, to 57.6 . Learning transfers to tasks not yet attempted without erasing gains on tasks already encountered. Experience improves efficiency as well: an agent with memory uses about 35 fewer model calls in comparison to zero-shot deployment. We conduct controlled experiments to isolate the effects of the model, its reasoning effort, and the harness's perception and motion interfaces. The choice of model has the largest effect. For example, 's success rate on RoboLab-120 is 82.8 with Opus 5.5, 51.6 with Haiku 5.5, and 35.2 with Opus 4.5. More reasoning helps all evaluated models. The value of additional harness support depends on the model. Weaker models are helped by assistive grasping and placing routines, while stronger models perform best without these routines. Stronger models also cope better with missing sensory information. With the harness, Opus 5.5 achieves a success rate of 82.8 with full sensory input, 81.1 without direct depth input, and 75.8 without depth or camera calibration. While the overall success rate does not suffer much, sensory impairment takes a toll on efficiency. The agent routes around limited sensory input by reconstructing 3D points via triangulation across views and, when needed, estimates camera calibration from images taken at known gripper poses. The mean number of model calls per episode rises from 34.8 with full sensory input to 46.3 without direct depth input and 53.5 without depth or camera calibration. A weaker model cannot compensate for impoverished perception: the success rate of with Haiku 5.5 on RoboLab-120 collapses from 51.6 with full sensory input to 10.7 without depth or camera calibration. Our experiments also indicate that replacing visual input with textual descriptions has a sharply detrimental effect, for example cutting the success rate of with Opus 5.5 from 82.8 to 36.8 ; this contrasts with prior work, which recommended replacing visual input with textual descriptions~ capx . Our results point to agentic manipulation policies as a promising foundation for generalist manipulation. AMPs are not yet practical, as the robot spends much of each episode waiting for the model to reason. But neither are the alternatives: the strongest VLA and WAM entries on the RoboLab-120 leaderboard at the time of writing succeed in 49.2 and 42.9 of the episodes, respectively, in contrast to 's 85.6 . A policy that fails every other task is not practical, however quickly it does so. We see a more promising path in making capable policies fast. Recent studies estimate that the cost of a given capability level has fallen by roughly an order of magnitude per year~ Gundlach2025,EmbersonRoodman2026 . A harness could further reduce waiting by reusing generated code, running feedback loops locally~ Liang2023,Huang2023:VoxPoser,Huang2026 , and planning the next motion while the current one executes~ Black2025:RTC . AMP experience could also be used to synthesize closed-loop onboard controllers~ Huang2026 or train compact models through distillation~ Shen2026:EmbodiedSWE,Liu2026:Guava . title: HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
summary: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation of 3D environments by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation rt2,openvla,pi0 . However, long-horizon robotic manipulation typically involve multiple interdependent manipulation steps, requiring robots to continuously track environmental states and retain historical interaction information wang2026sliding,dinh2026vision . Therefore, effective long-term memory mechanisms are crucial for improving the long-horizon robotic manipulation and cross-task generalization capabilities of VLA models. Most existing long-term memory mechanisms resemble episodic memory in the human brain, retaining extensive scene layouts, object states, and action outcomes from specific interactions, thereby providing rich information for robots to reuse historical experiences memoryvla,mem,map-vla,dejavu,memer . However, especially in complex 3D scenes, these episodic memory records also contain substantial details that are irrelevant to the current task or specific to particular scenarios (i.e., memory noise, as shown in Fig.~ fig:mem_noise ) and lack explicit guidance of generalizable manipulation patterns, resulting in limited transferability of experience across tasks echo . In contrast, humans possess an efficient memory system for interacting with 3D environments, which provides inspiration for addressing the aforementioned problem. Specifically, complementary learning systems (CLS) theory mcclelland1995there suggests that the hippocampus rapidly encodes and retains specific experiences, whereas the neocortex gradually develops generalizable semantic knowledge by integrating information across experiences. This division of labor enables the memory system to preserve information about specific events while identifying shared patterns across different experiences. Inspired by above mechanism, we propose HiMEM, a long-term memory framework for VLA models in 3D scenes. ~First, HiMEM introduces a meta-semantic memory consolidation method inspired by the complementary mechanisms of the hippocampus and neocortex. The hippocampus-inspired module identifies recurring manipulation patterns and their applicable conditions across different experiences. The neocortex-inspired module then consolidates these patterns into compact meta-semantic memories that represent environmental and object conditions, reusable manipulation strategies, and their success probabilities, enabling VLA models to derive a compact set of abstract guiding principles from extensive concrete manipulation experiences. ~Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that partially removes the corresponding episodic memories once relevant semantic memories have been established, thereby increasing the memory capacity limit. ~Finally, to address complex task scenarios, we introduce a mechanism for flexibly combining and utilizing multiple episodic and semantic memories. Specifically, meta-semantic memories provide manipulation patterns with conditional applicability, while episodic memories supplement information about specific manipulation procedures and state transitions. By incorporating visual observations of the current task, task instructions, and characteristics of the manipulated objects, the proposed mechanism flexibly combines memories at different levels of abstraction (i.e., episodic and semantic memories) to enable cross-scenario generalization in long-horizon tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that, across the four standard LIBERO suites, our method improves the average success rates of three mainstream memory-free VLA models, , , and OpenVLA-OFT, by 6.32, 3.65, and 2.15 percentage points, respectively. Compared with ECHO~ echo , HiMEM further improves the average success rates by 0.90, 1.17, and 0.57 percentage points on , , and OpenVLA-OFT, respectively. This paper substantially extends our NeurIPS 2026 conference paper, ECHO echo , to address long-horizon, complex spatial manipulation tasks in 3D environments. Building upon the original hierarchical episodic memory framework, this journal version further introduces semantic memory consolidation, episodic memory pruning, and joint utilization of episodic and semantic memories. The new contributions are summarized as follows: We propose a meta-semantic memory consolidation method inspired by the complementary mechanisms of the hippocampus and neocortex. Through cross-scenario statistical analysis, the method extracts shared patterns from manipulation experiences and organizes environmental conditions, object characteristics, manipulation strategies, and their execution success probabilities into compact semantic knowledge to enhance the transferability of experience across tasks. We propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes large amounts of content-similar episodic memories after the corresponding generalizable semantic memories have been established, thereby improving the storage efficiency and capacity of long-term memory. We propose a task-conditioned memory composition and utilization mechanism that integrates episodic and meta-semantic memories. Based on the characteristics of the current scenario and manipulated objects, this mechanism combines historical experiences at different levels of abstraction and provides guidance for action generation through step-by-step task planning, thereby supporting experience reuse under novel task combinations and manipulation conditions. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions. Existing approaches employ autoregressive action generation~ rt2,openvla , diffusion or flow-based policies~ diffusion-policy,octo,pi0 , and efficient action heads~ openvla-oft . Dual-system architectures further separate high-level reasoning from low-level action generation~ dpvla,robodual,fisvla . While these architectures advance robotic manipulation, long-horizon tasks require retaining and reusing historical information beyond the current observation. This motivates external memory mechanisms that complement VLA policies with persistent experience, supporting long-horizon execution and knowledge reuse across tasks. Memory for Long-Horizon Embodied Control Memory is essential for embodied control, as historical observations and experiences provide temporal context that may be absent from the current state~ rt1,chen2021decision,raea,statler . Recent studies explore different forms of memory representation and retrieval. MAP-VLA constructs stage-specific soft prompts from demonstrations and retrieves them through trajectory similarity~ map-vla . MemoryVLA integrates working memory with a persistent perceptual-cognitive memory bank, retrieving relevant representations and merging redundant entries~ memoryvla . MEM combines short-horizon video memory with long-horizon textual memory to capture events at different temporal and semantic scales~ mem . MemER selects task-relevant historical keyframes to support long-horizon robotic control~ memer . These methods demonstrate the importance of selecting, retaining, and reusing historical information. Beyond temporal dependencies within individual tasks, cross-task generalization further requires accumulating experiences across executions, organizing their outcomes, and extracting reusable knowledge from repeated interactions. Hierarchical Episodic Memory Organization Episodic memory preserves specific experiences, including observations, task contexts, and action trajectories. As experiences accumulate, flat memory structures provide limited explicit organization of general-to-specific relationships, complicating memory navigation and reuse. Hierarchical memory representations have therefore attracted increasing attention. For instance, Embodied-RAG organizes spatial and semantic information into a hierarchical semantic forest, supporting retrieval at different levels of abstraction~ embodied-rag . Hyperbolic embeddings provide a continuous geometric representation of hierarchical relationships~ rthe,poincare-emb . In particular, the Lorentz model supports hierarchical representation learning~ nickel2018learning , while entailment cones model asymmetric containment relations~ ganea2018hyperbolic . Building on these foundations, HiMEM focuses on the hierarchical organization of manipulation experiences. It organizes task-, subgoal-, and action-level episodic memories within a shared continuous hyperbolic tree, supporting hierarchical retrieval and incremental memory insertion. Both successful and failed experiences are retained as episodic evidence, providing a structured basis for subsequent knowledge consolidation. This distinction motivates episodic-to-semantic memory consolidation, through which detailed experiences are transformed into reusable knowledge. Existing embodied memory methods have explored redundancy reduction and semantic abstraction. title: Zero-Shot Benchmarking of Unified Multimodal Models for Shallow-Water UAV Image Distortion Assessment and Restoration
summary: Shallow-water UAV imagery provides centimeter-scale observations of benthic environments, but water-induced distortions complicate interpretation. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic zero-shot benchmark of unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for both assessing water-induced distortions and restoring shallow-water imagery within the same model framework. We evaluate five open-weight unified MLLMs with frozen pretrained weights and without access to paired reference images or descriptions of the true seabed. The benchmark contains 1,000 image pairs: 600 semi-synthetic UAV scenes created by applying synthetic water distortions to real shallow-water imagery and 400 fully synthetic through-water scenes. Three independent human annotations cover five distortion types. We evaluate four assessment prompts (P0-P3), from direct instruction to structured task decomposition, on all 1,000 images and four diagnosis-guided restoration prompts (R0-R3) on a common 100-image subset. Assessment varies substantially by model and prompt, with systematic prediction biases and a best pooled balanced accuracy of 0.654 for distortion presence. The best pooled PSNR gain is +0.255 dB, no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS, and some outputs alter scene structure or hallucinate content. Two restoration-only baselines also show limited transfer: InstructIR achieves a pooled PSNR gain of +0.040 dB, while PromptFix degrades all four pooled metrics under every prompt. Shallow-water UAV imagery provides centimeter-scale observations of benthic environments, but its interpretation is often degraded by water-induced distortions. Recent unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which combine image understanding and generation within a single architecture, offer a potential framework for both assessing and restoring these distortions. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic zero-shot benchmark of unified MLLMs that jointly assesses water-induced distortions and restores shallow-water imagery within the same model framework. Five open-weight unified MLLMs are evaluated with frozen pretrained weights and without access to paired reference images or descriptions of the true seabed. The benchmark contains 1,000 paired images, comprising 600 semi-synthetic UAV scenes generated by applying synthetic water distortions to real shallow-water imagery and 400 fully synthetic through-water scenes, with three independent human annotations of five distortion types. Four assessment prompts (P0--P3), ranging from direct instruction to structured task decomposition, are evaluated across all 1,000 images. Restoration is then evaluated on a common 100-image subset using four diagnosis-guided restoration prompts (R0--R3). Assessment is strongly model- and prompt-dependent, with a best pooled presence balanced accuracy of 0.654 and systematic prediction biases across models. Restoration is substantially less reliable: the best pooled PSNR gain is only ~dB, no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS, and some outputs introduce structural changes or hallucinated content. Two restoration-only baselines show similarly limited transfer, with InstructIR reaching only ~dB PSNR improvement and PromptFix degrading all four pooled metrics under every prompt. These results show that recognizing shallow-water degradation does not imply reliable physical restoration and establish a reproducible baseline for future multimodal assessment and restoration methods. Introduction sec:introduction hallow coastal waters host some of the most productive and most threatened ecosystems on Earth Hobohm2021 . Coral reefs, seagrass meadows, and tidal flats support fisheries honda2013habitat , buffer coastlines against storms guannel2016power , sequester carbon kinsey1991significance , and underpin the livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people, yet they are being degraded by climate change, sedimentation, and coastal development at an accelerating rate obura2019coral . Timely, repeatable observation of these environments is therefore essential for conservation planning, restoration prioritization, and coastal management, which has driven sustained investment in remote sensing of the shallow seafloor gonzalez2020monitoring, kroon2014informing . Remote sensing is the primary tool for observing shallow-water environments at scale, but the right platform depends on the trade-off between coverage and resolution he2024remote . Multispectral and hyperspectral satellites enable synoptic, repeat-pass mapping of coastal bathymetry and habitat over hundreds of kilometers duplancicleder2023optical , while airborne bathymetric surveys trade coverage for higher spatial and vertical accuracy kromer2025sea . Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) close the remaining resolution gap: flying tens of meters above the water, they resolve individual coral colonies and seagrass patches at centimeter-to-decimeter scale that satellites and crewed aircraft cannot match, at a fraction of the cost and with on-demand revisit scilla2025computer . This resolution advantage comes at the price of a much smaller footprint and, critically, a far greater sensitivity to the optical behavior of the water surface and column between the sensor and the seabed. Because UAV imagery is acquired close to the water at high spatial resolution, it inherits distortions that coarser satellite pixels tend to average away david_structure_motion_2021 . Building on our own characterization of shallow-water UAV imagery scilla2025computer,kromer2025sea , we consider five water-induced distortion types: (i) caustics, focused bright networks projected onto the seabed by a wavy air--water interface scilla2025computer ; (ii) sun glint, the specular reflection of the sun toward the sensor hedley2005sunglint ; (iii) refraction, the geometric displacement of submerged features at the air--water boundary agrafiotis2020correcting ; (iv) turbidity, the loss of contrast from light scattered by suspended sediment and organic matter cui2022water ; and (v) light absorption, the wavelength-dependent attenuation that progressively removes color and detail with depth ackleson2003light . Any UAV-based shallow-water application must contend with some combination of these five effects before the imagery is usable. Correcting these effects was first approached with physics-based computer vision. Image formation models borrowed from atmospheric dehazing, such as the dark channel prior he2011dark , and revised underwater-specific formulations that separately model backscatter and signal attenuation, such as Sea-thru akkaynak2019seathru , recover a physically plausible clean image by inverting an explicit optical model. These methods are interpretable and require no training data, but they rely on assumptions (homogeneous water, a single dominant distortion type, known depth or range) that rarely hold across the heterogeneous, multi-distortion scenes typical of shallow reefs. Deep learning relaxed these assumptions by learning the correction directly from data. Convolutional and generative-adversarial architectures such as FUnIE-GAN islam2020funie learn to map degraded underwater images to enhanced ones end to end and have been shown, across surveys of the field, to outperform hand-crafted priors on real and synthetic benchmarks anwar2020diving . However, most learned restorers are trained for a single degradation regime and a fixed output style, and their performance can degrade sharply outside the distribution of their training data, a persistent limitation for the varied optical conditions found in shallow coastal waters. Generative diffusion models have since become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity image restoration. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models ho2020ddpm and their efficient latent-space formulation underlying Stable Diffusion rombach2022ldm learn to invert a gradual noising process and can synthesize realistic detail that discriminative networks cannot, while more recent formulations such as ResShift yue2023resshift recast restoration as a residual-shifting diffusion process to cut sampling cost by an order of magnitude. Diffusion models are now being adapted directly to the underwater domain, for instance to enhance turbid and color-degraded scenes with physics-aware attention mechanisms zhang2024underwaterdiffusion , underscoring a broader shift from discriminative correction toward generative restoration. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) add a capability that none of the above methods have: the ability to reason about and describe an image's degradation in natural language before acting on it. Vision-language systems such as GPT-4V openai2023gpt4v and LLaVA liu2023llava exhibit in-context learning, adapting their behavior to a task from instructions and examples in the prompt alone, without retraining dong2023icl . This has motivated recent work that prompts MLLMs directly for image quality assessment wu2024mllmiqa , and has exposed a complication: MLLM outputs are highly sensitive to how a prompt is phrased and structured sahoo2024prompt,ismithdeen2025promptception . Chain-of-thought and zero-shot reasoning prompts can partially stabilize this sensitivity wei2022chain,kojima2022large . More recently, benchmarks such as MME-Unify, GIR-Bench, and RealUnify have begun to evaluate whether unified models can effectively connect their understanding and generation capabilities xie2026mmeunify,li2026girbench,shi2026realunify . Their results reveal persistent limitations in transferring reasoning or understanding into faithful generation, despite both capabilities being integrated within the same model. Whether this coupling is sufficient for scientific image restoration under a strictly zero-shot, reference-free protocol remains largely unexplored, particularly for shallow-water UAV imagery. Recent work has begun to explore related directions in underwater imaging. UQ-Bench evaluates MLLMs for underwater image-quality perception, including distortion recognition, free-text description, and quality scoring under a zero-shot setting cao2026uq . However, its scope is limited to assessment and does not investigate whether the same models can generate restored imagery. In parallel, degradation-aware conditioning has been introduced for underwater image enhancement. CPLDP uses learned prompts representing color casts, uneven illumination, and haze to guide a task-specific enhancement network yao2026conditional , while DIE2UIE extracts degradation- and semantic-aware visual-language cues to adaptively guide underwater enhancement wang2026degradation . These approaches demonstrate the value of explicitly connecting degradation perception with enhancement, but rely on task-specific trained restoration frameworks rather than the pretrained generative capability of a unified MLLM. This gap motivates our work. We present the first zero-shot benchmark of unified MLLMs for both the assessment and restoration of shallow-water UAV imagery within a single locally hosted model, without delegating diagnosis or synthesis to a separate network. Every experiment in this study is conducted strictly zero-shot and without reference supervision: all five models are evaluated with their pretrained weights kept entirely frozen, no fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, or in-context exemplars are used, and no model is ever shown the paired reference image, a restoration example, or any description of the true seabed, either in its prompt or otherwise. Each prediction is produced from a single distorted image and a text instruction alone; the reference image is used only afterward, by us, to score the outputs. Our contributions are the following: (i) We curate and annotate a 1,000-image benchmark spanning two complementary sources: 600 semi-synthetic UAV scenes obtained by applying synthetic water distortions to real ground-truth imagery (KAUSTics dataset scilla2026kaustics ), and 400 fully synthetic through-water scenes (Sea-Undistort dataset kromer2025sea ), with three independent expert ratings of all five distortion types per image. (ii) We design four progressively structured, zero-shot prompts for assessment and four for restoration, spanning direct, role-conditioned, definition-guided, and reasoning-guided variants, none of which reference ground truth, to systematically quantify how prompt design alone affects both distortion assessment and restoration quality.
